report:
**Conclusion:** Yes. EMDR can alleviate PTSD symptoms and is an evidence-based trauma-focused psychotherapy. Systematic-review evidence finds EMDR reduces PTSD symptoms; a major review concluded that EMDR and trauma-focused CBT can be recommended as first-line psychological treatments, although cognitive processing therapy, cognitive therapy, and prolonged exposure had particularly strong evidence bases. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32284821/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32284821/)

Major guidelines support its use, with some differences in strength and scope. NICE recommends EMDR as an option for adults with PTSD or clinically important symptoms more than three months after **non-combat-related** trauma. [https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116/chapter/Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng116/chapter/Recommendations) The U.S. VA’s National Center for PTSD describes many studies supporting EMDR’s effectiveness when delivered over roughly three months and notes that multiple PTSD guidelines give it a strong recommendation. [https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/emdr_pro.asp](https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/txessentials/emdr_pro.asp)

EMDR is not guaranteed to work for every person, and it should be delivered by a properly trained clinician after assessment of the person’s trauma history, symptoms, safety, and preferences. Other trauma-focused therapies—especially prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy—are also well-supported options. The APA characterizes its recommendation for EMDR as conditional, reflecting uncertainty in comparative evidence and the need to individualize treatment. [https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/emdr-therapy-ptsd](https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/emdr-therapy-ptsd)
